mean: to slack off chatting when one should be working

story.text: As the expression is traditionally explained, in the Edo period peddlers went door to door selling hair oil. The oil was thick and dripped slowly from the measuring ladle into the customer's container, so the sellers chatted with their customers while they waited. To onlookers they seemed to be gossiping instead of working, and 'selling oil' came to mean idling away time that should be spent on work.

bad.s: 体育[たいいく]の先生[せんせい]が、校庭[こうてい]にチョークで{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the PE teacher drew a line on the playground in chalk)
bad.why: It is never a literal line. To draw a line on the ground, say sen o hiita.

bad.s: 友人[ゆうじん]の冗談[じょうだん]は{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]して}、相手[あいて]を怒[おこ]らせた。
bad.en: (meant: my friend's joke crossed the line and made the other person angry)
bad.why: Crossing a line is issen o koeru. Issen o kakusu means standing clearly apart from something.

mean: a cut above, one step ahead
lit: one rank higher (the counter 'mai' here counts ranks, as on a ranking list): just a notch above the other side

use.how: Always comparing two sides: AのほうがBより一枚上手だ, 相手が一枚上手だった. Says one side has a slight edge in skill or cunning, often in a contest of wits.

near.diff: 一目置く is respecting someone as better than you; 一枚上手 describes the side that is slightly ahead.

cue: You set up a clever April Fool's prank on your sister, but she saw it coming and turned it back on you. Admit who won.

ctx.s: 将棋[しょうぎ]では、兄[あに]のほうが僕[ぼく]より{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だ。
ctx.en: At shogi, my older brother is a notch better than me.

ctx.s: 「いたずらを仕掛[しか]けたつもりが、妹[いもうと]のほうが{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だったよ。」
ctx.en: "I thought I was pranking my sister, but she was one step ahead of me."

ctx.s: 交渉[こうしょう]では相手[あいて]が{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}で、こちらの条件[じょうけん]はほとんど通[とお]らなかった。
ctx.en: The other side outmanoeuvred us in the negotiations, and hardly any of our terms got through.

ctx.s: 決勝[けっしょう]では、経験[けいけん]で{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}のベテランが勝[か]った。
ctx.en: In the final, the veteran, who had the edge in experience, won.

ctx.s: 逃[に]げ切[き]れると思[おも]っていた詐欺師[さぎし]より、刑事[けいじ]のほうが{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だった。
ctx.en: The con man thought he'd get away, but the detective was one step ahead of him.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]を出[だ]し抜[ぬ]こうなんて無理[むり]だよ。いつも{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}なんだから。」
ctx.en: "There's no way you'll outsmart her. She's always a step ahead."

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}にピアノを弾[ひ]く。
bad.en: (meant: he plays the piano skilfully)
bad.why: It is not an adverb of skill (here the kanji are read uwate, not jouzu). It only compares two sides: kare no hou ga ichimai uwate da.

bad.s: 世界[せかい]チャンピオンは、素人[しろうと]の僕[ぼく]より{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the world champion is vastly better than an amateur like me)
bad.why: It means a slight edge between near-equals. For a huge gap, say ashimoto ni mo oyobanai or kaku ga chigau.
